Ostrich Island, developed and published by MeDungeon Ltd., is a curious mix of adventure, platforming, and light exploration that places players in control of an ostrich stranded in a chain of islands following a volcanic catastrophe. It is a game that embraces absurdity from the very beginning, using its strange premise not as a joke, but as a foundation for a surprisingly layered and atmospheric experience. Beneath its humorous concept lies a game that encourages curiosity, patience, and discovery, all while balancing lighthearted charm with subtle challenge. It feels both like an old-school collect-a-thon and a leisurely exploration sim, inviting players to dig through every corner of its tropical and mysterious world in search of secrets.

The opening levels of Ostrich Island set the tone for what follows. You find yourself on an idyllic island surrounded by the soft crash of waves and scattered remnants of civilization. There is no urgency—no timer, no immediate threat—just a sense of wonder. As an ostrich, you can run, jump, kick, and even bury your head in the sand, each mechanic serving both functional and comedic purposes. What at first seems like a novelty—playing as a bird not exactly known for grace or heroism—gradually becomes the source of the game’s identity. The controls are deliberately a bit clumsy, reflecting the awkward gait of an ostrich, but they are responsive enough to make platforming and exploration satisfying. Collectibles are scattered everywhere: hidden eggs, shells, coins, and hats that unlock cosmetic customization. Each discovery gives a small jolt of satisfaction, especially when unearthing hidden areas or triggering secret interactions within the environment.

Progression in Ostrich Island unfolds through a series of connected islands that each introduce new mechanics or challenges. You can dive underwater, leap across cliffs, and occasionally solve small puzzles to unlock new routes. The game includes a light RPG-like progression system where you can upgrade abilities such as jumping height or swimming stamina, allowing you to revisit earlier levels to reach previously inaccessible areas. This lends the experience a touch of the “Metroidvania” formula, encouraging backtracking in pursuit of completion. The exploration feels organic—there are no strict missions or linear objectives, just a simple loop of discovery and collection that grows deeper the more you engage with it. The addition of experience points and unlockable skills adds a sense of progression that keeps the pacing balanced, though the repetitive nature of tasks can occasionally set in after several hours of play.

The world design deserves special mention for its tone and atmosphere. The islands are diverse, shifting from bright tropical beaches to shadowy underwater caves and volcanic ruins. Each level contains environmental storytelling elements—crashed boats, abandoned relics, or ruins that hint at some lost civilization—giving a quiet sense of mystery beneath the silliness of playing as an ostrich. Despite the game’s simplicity, there is a striking beauty to its low-poly art style. The lighting is soft, the colors vibrant, and the environments feel alive even without bustling activity. The developers use subtle environmental cues like fluttering butterflies, gentle waves, and ambient soundscapes to create a tranquil rhythm, making exploration both relaxing and rewarding. While the visuals won’t impress on a technical level, their cohesive style and charm make the game visually memorable.

As the adventure progresses, the tone takes an unexpected shift when you begin exploring darker underground sections filled with hostile skeletons and traps. These sudden bursts of danger add tension but also disrupt the earlier serenity. Some players may find this change welcome, as it introduces a challenge and variation to the gameplay, while others may feel it clashes with the otherwise calming atmosphere. Combat is minimal, mostly revolving around using the ostrich’s “kick” ability, but the encounters are designed more for surprise than strategy. The game occasionally suffers from uneven pacing in these later levels, where platforming precision and enemy attacks can become frustrating due to the occasionally awkward physics. Still, the unpredictability of these sequences helps maintain engagement through variety, even if they don’t always feel fully balanced.

Ostrich Island’s greatest strength lies in its sense of humor and personality. The very concept of playing as an ostrich surviving a volcanic disaster is inherently absurd, yet the game treats it with sincerity. Every movement, from the comical running animation to the exaggerated kicking motion, carries a whimsical charm. Even the collectible hats and costumes reinforce the playful tone, allowing players to dress their ostrich in ridiculous combinations that make exploration feel more personal. It’s a game that never takes itself too seriously, and that levity keeps it enjoyable even when the mechanics falter or repetition sets in.

The soundtrack complements the mood perfectly, featuring mellow tunes that blend tropical rhythms with ambient background sounds. It creates a laid-back atmosphere ideal for wandering and collecting without pressure. The audio design supports immersion rather than seeking attention—waves lap gently against the shore, birds call in the distance, and the crunch of sand underfoot feels oddly soothing. It’s the kind of experience best enjoyed in small, quiet sessions, where you can absorb its playful world at a relaxed pace.

One of the game’s more ambitious features is its inclusion of a level editor and Steam Workshop support, allowing players to create and share their own islands. This adds considerable replay value and expands the game beyond its modest core campaign. The built-in customization options for the ostrich—ranging from visual changes to new skins—further enhance the sense of individuality and fun. The community-driven aspect has allowed the game to live beyond its original release, turning it into a small but enduring sandbox for creative players who enjoy lighthearted exploration.

Despite its simplicity, Ostrich Island manages to capture something rare—a balance between humor and atmosphere. It’s not a polished masterpiece, and it occasionally feels rough around the edges, with uneven pacing, control quirks, and repetitive objectives. But its sincerity and inventiveness make it stand out in a crowded field of indie platformers. There’s a genuine sense of discovery woven into its design, one that rewards curiosity rather than skill or precision. It’s a game that asks you to slow down, to enjoy the absurd, and to find joy in small victories—whether it’s uncovering a hidden egg, kicking open a treasure chest, or simply standing at the edge of a cliff watching the sunset. Ostrich Island may not soar to great heights, but it struts confidently in its own delightful and peculiar way.

I am 32 years old.

My ex-wife and I have a daughter together, and we adopted our son together. Both are now 4 years old.

When we were going through our separation, I felt lost and unhappy. I was self-destructive. One day, I was so angry with everything spiraling out of control that I punched a concrete wall in a moment of overwhelming emotion. This resulted in breaking my fifth metacarpal in my right hand—the hand I worked with, played games with, and used to carry my children to bed—the hand I desperately needed to ensure I could continue providing.

Upon learning the severity of the self-inflicted damage, I became almost suicidal. Keep in mind that just a few months before this, I was the happiest man, with no history of depression or anxiety. I had never experienced anger outbursts, nor was I the type to break down and cry, but I was in a tough situation that truly prevented me from seeing the light on the other side.

With nothing better to do, I looked for a game I could play WITH ONE HAND while recovering. Somehow, I stumbled upon this game and read some of the comments. I decided it was worth a try... I must admit I didn't beat the game, nor did I play as much as some of you. In fact, I may have played this game for only a day or two. That being said, after doing so, I had a new joy and hope for life. I managed to leave behind the pain and suffering that had been thrust upon me. I could experience the joy and happiness of other people. I relaxed for 5 ♥♥♥♥ minutes listening to this music, long enough to realize that I would be okay.

After realizing this, I turned off the game and went back to work. My hand hurt a lot, but I was motivated. I stopped feeling so sorry for myself and became the father I needed to be at that moment, not the weak boy I was behaving like.

Today, I am close friends with the mother of my children. We don't fight, argue, or say hurtful things to each other. We are parents and friends.

Now I have 3 children. My third child is, wait, ALSO 4 YEARS OLD. The woman I am with was going through a very similar situation at the time of my separation, and we just unexpectedly stumbled into each other's lives. We have been dating for a year and are very happy together.

Moral of the story: you never know what life has in store for you, and if I had given up when all odds were against me, I wouldn't be where I am today. This silly little game helped me realize that.

Thank you.

I thought the sheer absurdity of this would make it a good experience. It looked so weird from the outside; what's the worst it could be?

Turns out, it steps on its own potential. The large, varied island environments are actually real fun to explore, but you're on a time limit and movement does not feel fluid. It's not the worst I've played, but it doesn't match the urgency of completing each island . 

There is the ability to kick things, and seeing how they react is honestly fun and likable. The issue is that the kick stops all your movement, takes ridiculously long, and the buildup for it doesn't match the relative nudge of whatever you're kicking. If you could keep a little momentum, and if you could choose between a quick kick that matches the effect of what's in the game now, or a slow kick that takes as long as kicks do in this game now but sends things flying or knocks them over harder, I'd say this game could be ridiculous fun.

I will say collecting things actually feels satisfying. Eggs in particular, and just points from kicking stuff. A clever move on the developers' part for putting this temptation in; if only the kicking didn't actually feel cumbersome and impeding when we really are trying to get off the island, too.

I say "No" here, but that's for my tastes. If anyone likes this premise, give it a shot and see if it fits you. Maybe you've gotten it in a way this non-gamer doesn't. Just be sure to remember that Steam refund option.

"Ostrich Island" oyuncuların bir devekuşu rolünü üstlendiği benzersiz bir macera/keşif/RPG oyunudur. Oyun bir yanardağın patlaması ve hazırlıksız yakalanan bir devekuşu hariç takımadaların tüm sakinlerinin tahliye edilmesiyle başlar. Oyuncunun görevi devekuşunun kaçmasına ve ailesiyle yeniden bir araya gelmesine yardımcı olmaktır.

Oyunda tropik cennetler, fırtınalı bölgeler, okyanusun derinlikleri ve yeraltı mağaraları gibi keşfedilecek çeşitli ortamlar bulunmaktadır. Her ada keşfedilmeyi bekleyen gizli başarılar, koleksiyonlar ve bonuslarla doludur. Oyuncular şapka takabilir, fotoğraf çekmek için bir fotoğraf makinesi bulabilir, kelebek yakalayabilir, nesneleri tekmeleyerek çevreyle etkileşime girebilir ve gizli adaları tek başlarına veya bir arkadaşlarıyla birlikte ortaya çıkarabilirler. Ek olarak, oyuncular tavuk arkadaşlarını yetiştirip besleyerek oyunun derinliğine ve sırlarına katkıda bulunabilirler.

Oyuncular ilerledikçe deneyim puanları kazanır, seviye atlar ve yeni beceri ve yeteneklerin kilidini açarlar. Oyun tamamlandığında, daha zorlu bir Game+ modu kullanılabilir hale gelir. Oyuncular ayrıca Yuva'yı ziyaret edebilir, burada yolculukları sırasında yaptıkları eşyaları ve keşifleri görüntüleyebilir ve hatırlayabilir, devekuşunun ailesi hakkında daha fazla bilgi edinebilirler.

Kendini yaratıcı hissedenler için oyun, oyuncuların devekuşları için yeni görünümler oluşturabilecekleri ve hatta tüm adaları tasarlayabilecekleri bir Atölye özelliği sunuyor. Bu kreasyonlar toplulukla paylaşılabilir ve oyuncular devekuşlarını daha da özelleştirmek veya oyun deneyimlerini geliştirmek için diğer kullanıcılar tarafından yapılan içerikleri de indirebilirler.

"Ostrich Island", oyuncuların bir devekuşuna çeşitli ortamlarda rehberlik ettiği, sırları ortaya çıkardığı ve keşif dolu keyifli bir yolculuğa çıktığı benzersiz ve tuhaf bir macera sunuyor.

This was quite an interesting experience of a game to play through; with some decent visuals and less than stellar controls, this is a game I wouldn't normally recommend, in fact I would have likely given this a negative review. However due to some of the after-game collectibles, customize wearable skins and hats you can find, and even an option to start raising your own chicken in the previous stages. You get quite a bit more to do after you complete all the stages. Thankfully there is a bit more that makes this an oddly good game for me. The music itself is nice and atmospheric, the in game lore is not needed but well appreciated with the Ostrich character having relatives and family members well known for certain traits, and the sluggish movement with the very shortly linear stage layouts, helps the game and not make it overstay it's welcome. With all that said, I can see why people would dislike this game, it is greatly lacking in a lot of areas when compared to higher budgeted indie games or triple A titles. And Heck, it's even crashed on me during two occasions (though closing out of the game and reopening it sorts everything out). It does indeed have quite a broad amount of problems, but that's to be expected with some indie games, And like with most indie games I'm not as harsh on them as I would be to games with massive amounts of production value put into them. So at the end of the day, I would classify this as a bad indie game. But I am biased when it comes to birds being used as playable characters and being able to explore stages to discover more hidden collectibles. This is not a game I'd recommend to anyone, I'd only say you should give this a shot if you have a lot of patience, like in game collecting and have a big interest with Caribbean themed environments. If you qualify for these exceptions, then I'd recommend you buy and give it a try. You may have a soft spot for this game like I have. It's certainly grown on me after playing for 15 hours. I now see "Ostrich Island" as a Guilty Pleasure for me. ^_^
